title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXV
paragraphs:
“Then went the jury out whose names were Mr. Blindman, Mr. No-good, Mr.
Malice, Mr. Love-lust, Mr. Live-loose, Mr. Heady, Mr. High-mind, Mr.
Enmity, Mr. Liar, Mr. Cruelty, Mr. Hate-light, Mr. Implacable, who
every one gave in his private verdict against him among themselves, and
afterwards unanimously concluded to bring him in guilty before the
judge. And first among themselves, Mr. Blindman, the foreman, said, I
see clearly that this man is a heretic. Then said Mr. No-good, Away
with such a fellow from the earth! Ay, said Mr. Malice, for I hate the
very look of him. Then said Mr. Love-lust, I could never endure him.
Nor I, said Mr. Live-loose; for he would be always condemning my way.
Hang him, hang him, said Mr. Heady. A sorry scrub, said Mr. High-mind.
My heart riseth against him, said Mr. Enmity. He is a rogue, said Mr.
Liar. Hanging is too good for him, said Mr. Cruelty. Let us despatch
him out of the way said Mr. Hate-light. Then said Mr. Implacable, Might
I have all the world given me, I could not be reconciled to him;
therefore let us forthwith bring him in guilty of death.”—_Pilgrim’s
Progress_.

When the immortal Bunyan pictures the persecuting passions delivering their guilty verdict, who feels pity for Faithful? To know oneself innocent before a condemning crowd, to be certain that only the good in us is being denounced, is a rare and blessed fate denied even to some of the greatest men. The truly pitiable man cannot call himself a martyr, even if he persuades himself that those stoning him are merely ugly passions in human form. He knows they stone him not for declaring what is right, but for failing to be the man he claimed to be.

This awareness was withering Bulstrode as he prepared to leave Middlemarch and end his wounded life in that melancholy refuge, the indifference of unfamiliar faces. His wife’s dutiful, merciful faithfulness had relieved one terror. Yet her presence remained a court before which he shrank from confessing and longed for someone to plead his case. His evasive arguments with himself over Raffles’s death had preserved his conception of the all-knowing Being to whom he prayed. But terror prevented him from exposing those arguments to judgment in a full confession to his wife. The acts he had washed and diluted in inward reasoning and motives, for which invisible forgiveness seemed comparatively easy to obtain—what would she call them? He could not bear the thought that, even silently, she might call them Murder. Her uncertainty sheltered him. Knowing she could not yet feel justified in pronouncing that worst condemnation gave him strength to face her. Someday, perhaps when he was dying, he would tell her everything. In that deepening shadow, as she held his hand in the gathering darkness, perhaps she could listen without shrinking from his touch. Perhaps. But concealment had been his lifelong habit, and the impulse to confess was powerless against the fear of deeper humiliation.

He treated his wife with anxious tenderness, not simply because he dreaded a harsh judgment from her, but because her suffering caused him profound distress. She had sent their daughters to a boarding school on the coast to conceal the crisis from them as much as possible. Their absence freed her from the intolerable need to explain her grief or watch their frightened bewilderment. She could now live openly with the sorrow that daily streaked her hair with white and left her eyelids heavy.

“Tell me anything you would like me to do, Harriet,” Bulstrode had said. “I mean about the arrangements for our property. I intend to keep the land I own around here and leave it to you as a secure provision. If you have any wishes in these matters, please don’t hide them.”
A few days later, after returning from a visit to her brother’s house, she began speaking to her husband about a subject she had been considering for some time.

“I _would_ like to help my brother’s family, Nicholas. I think we owe Rosamond and her husband some amends. Walter says Mr. Lydgate will have to leave town. His practice is worth almost nothing, and they have very little to set themselves up elsewhere. I’d gladly give up something of our own to make amends to my poor brother’s family.”

Mrs. Bulstrode did not want to approach the facts more closely than “make amends”; she knew her husband must understand. For a particular reason unknown to her, her suggestion made him wince. He hesitated before replying—

“We can’t carry out your wish in that way, my dear. Mr. Lydgate has effectively refused any further help from me. He has repaid the thousand pounds I lent him. Mrs. Casaubon advanced him the money for that purpose. This is his letter.”

The letter seemed to wound Mrs. Bulstrode deeply. The reference to Mrs. Casaubon’s loan reflected the public feeling that naturally everyone would avoid any connection with her husband. She remained silent for some time. Tears fell one after another, her chin shaking as she wiped them away. Sitting opposite, Bulstrode ached to see that grief-worn face, so bright and blooming only two months before. It had aged to accompany his own withered features in sadness. Driven to attempt some comfort, he said—

“There is another way I could help your brother’s family, Harriet, if you’re willing to take part. It would benefit you as well, I think: it would be a good arrangement for managing the land I intend you to have.”

“Garth once considered taking charge of Stone Court and putting your nephew Fred there. The stock would stay as it is, and instead of ordinary rent they would pay an agreed share of the profits. Combined with his work under Garth, that would give the young man a good start. Would that please you?”
“Yes, it would,” Mrs. Bulstrode answered with renewed energy. “Poor Walter is so dejected. Before leaving, I would try anything in my power to help him. We’ve always been brother and sister.”

“You must put the proposal to Garth yourself, Harriet,” Mr. Bulstrode said. He disliked saying what followed, but wanted the arrangement for reasons beyond comforting his wife. “Tell him the land is effectively yours and he need have no dealings with me. Everything can pass through Standish. I mention it because Garth resigned as my agent. I can give you a paper he drew up himself, setting out the terms. You can ask him to accept them again. I think he may agree when you propose it for your nephew’s sake.”
